paras: The Forest parlor assault was an attack on an unnamed Black man at Forest, Mississippi, in about late January or early February 1903, after he sat down in the parlor of Capt. S. B. Fairchild and refused to leave. Friends summoned by telephone handled him roughly and took him to jail, and the account says he came near being hanged before the sheriff interfered. The incident is known only from a press dispatch that presented it as a consequence of the "Roosevelt-Hays policy".

The dispatch, sent from Jackson and credited to the Advocate, paired the Forest incident with one at Clinton, Mississippi, where a Black woodcutter was said to have washed his hands in a family's bowl and prepared to eat dinner in the house. It offered both cases as evidence of "what effect the Indianola postoffice incident is having on the negroes of the State."

According to the dispatch, "a big, burley negro" walked into Fairchild's parlor and took a seat in the presence of Fairchild's wife and daughter. When the family ordered him to leave, he would not, and a telephone message brought "a number of friends" to the house. The man was "roughly handled from there to jail," where he was lodged "thanks to the interference of the sheriff." The dispatch said that both the Forest and Clinton men had "come near stretching hemp" and would have been hanged but for "some of the older heads."
The coverage does not name the man, describe his injuries, or report any charge against him or what became of him after he was jailed. No action against the men who seized him is reported.

The only known report appeared on February 14, 1903, in the New Iberia Enterprise and Independent Observer of Louisiana, under the editorial heading "Some More of the Fruits." The editor introduced the dispatch as "showing the fruits of the Roosevelt-Hays policy" and called the two men "candidates for 'glory' by the grape vine route."
No Mississippi paper's report of the Forest incident, and no Black-press coverage of it, was found.

accounts.label: Jackson press dispatch (credited to the Advocate) in a Louisiana editorial
accounts.gist: A Black man sat in Capt. Fairchild's parlor before his wife and daughter and would not leave; friends called by telephone handled him roughly to jail, and only the sheriff's interference and 'older heads' kept him from being hanged.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Some More of the Fruits,' the editorial calls the two men 'candidates for "glory" by the grape vine route,' blames the Roosevelt-Hays policy and the Indianola postoffice incident, and treats the man's conduct, not the assault, as the offense.

record_check.dossier: Within the week before a Jackson dispatch reprinted 1903-02-14; plausibly late January to early February 1903
Sitting in a white family's parlor before the women and refusing to leave (a racial offense, not a crime charge)
The man's presence in the parlor and refusal to leave; editorial attributes it to Roosevelt's 'policy' and the Indianola postoffice incident
'A number of friends' of the Fairchild household, summoned by telephone

record_check.record: The dispatch says a hanging was narrowly avoided.
record_check.dossier: The dispatch says both the Forest and Clinton men 'came near stretching hemp'; the explicit 'came near being a hanging sure enough' refers to the Clinton case
Not in custody when seized; the mob took him to jail, where he was lodged through the sheriff's interference
